name: L'Anse aux Meadows
hook: Overgrown ridges in Newfoundland were a Norse camp of c. AD 1000, the first authenticated in North America.
claim: Helge Ingstad and archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad claimed that overgrown ridges at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, were the remains of a Norse settlement of about AD 1000, physical evidence of the Vinland voyages told in Icelandic sagas.

claimed_age.label: c. AD 1000 (saga chronology)
claimed_age.basis: Not a measured date: the sagas' chronology of voyages c. AD 1000, called the 'assumed historical age of ca AD 1000' in S2.

accepted_age.label: AD 1021 (felling of 3 worked wood items; 14C wiggle-match)
accepted_age.basis: 127 14C measurements on 83 rings from 4 Norse-cut wood items (3 datable), matched to the AD 993 spike. Occupation length unsettled: years (S5) or up to a century (S9).

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Norse voyages to 'Vinland' c. AD 1000 were widely accepted from the sagas, but Vinland's location was disputed and no incontrovertible Norse site was known.

unambiguous_signal.note: In 1960 there were only ridges that 'looked as if they might be building remains'. Digging from 1961 exposed Iceland/Greenland-type sod houses and Norse finds; exact find years unconfirmed.

documented_context.note: Buildings, hearths and finds were excavated and recorded in place from 1961 by a professional team; other occupations had to be separated from the Norse remains (see notes).

multiple_dating_methods.note: In 1960-65 the age rested on house and artifact comparison with Iceland and Greenland (typology, not counted here; S1). Nydal's earliest cited 14C date list is 1970.

multiple_labs.note: S2 lists Trondheim (T-) and Stockholm (St-) dates, but its earliest cited date list is from 1970; no source found on which labs had reported by 1965.

professional_recovery.note: Archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad directed the archaeological work on all seven expeditions (1961-68), with archaeologists from Norway, Iceland, Sweden and the US (S7).

peer_reviewed_report.note: Publications by 1965 listed by Cooke are short or popular: H. Ingstad's Arctic Circular note (issued 1963) and a 1964 National Geographic article. The full report came in 1977 (S2).

material_accessible.note: No source found on whether outside scholars could inspect the site or finds in 1960-65.

independent_teams.note: Archaeologists from Norway, Iceland, Sweden and the US took part, but within the Ingstads' own expeditions; no separately run team is documented for 1960-65.

proponent_stake.note: No commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented in sources read. H. Ingstad, an explorer-author, had argued before the find that the Norse reached Canada (S2).

objections.text: The houses might have been built by Indigenous people rather than the Norse; many groups lived at the site over 4,000-5,000 years (S7).
objections.raised_by: Unnamed early suggestion, reported by JSTOR Daily
objections.outcome_note: Handmade iron nails ended this suggestion (S10); iron slag and boat rivets did most to identify the site as Norse (S7). Local Indigenous groups then made no metal tools (S1).

objections.text: Radiocarbon dates on charcoal could read too old because the settlers burned driftwood or other long-dead ('old') wood.
objections.outcome_note: Nydal built a 30±20-year old-wood error into AD 975-1020; Kuitems et al. found legacy dates spread over the Viking Age. The bias limited precision but never bore on Norse identity.

status_note: The site's Norse identity is not in dispute; Ledger et al. (2019) call it the only undisputed pre-1492 European site in the Americas. Its function, length of use and saga place-name remain debated.
what_settled_it: The Ingstads' 1961-68 excavations found eight sod buildings of Iceland/Greenland type, iron slag and boat rivets, a bronze ring-headed pin and a spindle whorl. The national heritage board backed designation in 1968; UNESCO listing and dating studies (1989, 2022) later confirmed it.

timeline.event: Rafn opens a spirited scholarly debate over where the Norse reached America; Torfaeus (1705) and Forster (1784) had speculated earlier.
Local resident George Decker leads explorer Helge Ingstad to overgrown ridges at L'Anse aux Meadows that look like building remains.
First of seven Ingstad expeditions (1961-68); archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad directs the excavation.
H. Ingstad's note 'Discovery of Vinland' appears in the Arctic Circular (vol. 15 no. 1, dated 1962, issued January 1963).
National Geographic publishes H. Ingstad's 'Vinland ruins prove Vikings found the New World'.
Excavations end. The Historic Sites and Monuments Board's 1968 minutes back designation as the first known Viking site in North America.
Anne Stine Ingstad publishes the full excavation report, The Discovery of a Norse Settlement in America (Oslo).
Nydal's review of the radiocarbon series, allowing for driftwood and old-wood error, calibrates the occupation to AD 975-1020.
Wallace argues the site is the sagas' Straumfjord, a base for voyages farther south.
Ledger et al. report a new cultural horizon in the adjacent bog; re-analysis of legacy dates suggests Norse activity may have lasted a century.
Kuitems et al. date the felling of three Norse-cut wood items to AD 1021 using the AD 993 cosmic-ray radiocarbon spike.

decisive_tests.test: Survey, by permitted archaeologists, of the Miramichi region of New Brunswick (Wallace's candidate for the saga's Hop) for short-lived Norse camps.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether L'Anse aux Meadows was a base for sites farther south, as Wallace (2003) argues from the sagas and the finds.

decisive_tests.test: Date the cultural horizon Ledger et al. (2019) found in the bog beside the ruins with single-year 14C on seeds or worked wood, and identify who left it.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether Norse activity lasted a few years (Wallace 2003) or up to a century (Ledger 2019), and whether the horizon is Norse or Indigenous.

falsifier: Evidence that the diagnostic finds (iron rivets and slag, ring-headed pin, spindle whorl) are intrusive, or that the sod buildings and metal-cut wood are later European work, would overturn this status.

confidence_note: Core facts read in S1, S2, S5, S7 and S8. Weak spots: find years within 1961-68, when the first 14C dates were run, and outside access to the site in 1960-65.
corrections: Brief: 'The claim that Norse voyagers of the Vinland sagas reached North America'. By 1960 few informed scholars doubted Norse voyages c. AD 1000; what was new was a physical Norse site (Cooke 1965, S6).
notes: George Decker, a local man, led H. Ingstad to the ridges (S7). year_resolved 1968 is a judgment call; acceptance by c. 1965 is possible but unverified. No named critic of the Norse identification was found, so key_critics is empty; no hoax has been alleged. Mixing: Norse wood is identified by deposit and metal-tool cuts (S1); shore pits of possible native use were left out of the mean age (S2); a Point Revenge point lies in the A-B-C complex and Innu camped among the ruins in the 18th-19th c. (S5). Matching the site to a saga place (Straumfjord, S5; 'could be', S8) is interpretive. Kay (S4) studies function, not identity. Methods (4): architecture, artifacts, ironworking, 14C.

open_issues: year_claimed kept at 1960 as instructed (site identified: S2, S7). No 1960 public statement found; earliest verified publication is H. Ingstad's Arctic Circular note, issued Jan 1963 (via S6; no DOI/URL, so not a source).
Dropped the 'prior' objection (doubt that a Norse site would be found): no named, sourced raiser was found, as the review allowed.
Saga-place identification moved to notes, not objections: no sourced sceptic of Wallace's Straumfjord/Leifsbudir identification was found.
UNESCO inscription year (1978) left out: whc.unesco.org returned HTTP 403 and no Parks Canada page read gave the year.
S3 volume left as Crossref's '201'; the DOI suggests Special Volume 2 but the publisher page could not be read. S5 page range (5-43 per review) not confirmed, so omitted.

Find years of the pin and spindle whorl (whorl reportedly 1964) unconfirmed, so unambiguous_signal is 'partial'. The identification objection's raiser is unnamed (S10). S11 (A.S. Ingstad 1977) not read.
No objection recorded for a later-European origin of the ruins: no source raising it was found.
D19 re-rating 2026-09-23: unchanged — vindicated fits: the Norse settlement is undisputed; debates on its function, length of use and saga place-name are details, not the core claim.
